News.title: France MUST stop the boats, stop the excuses and start delivering what British taxpayers are paying for
News.content:
Towtally wrong

IT’S barely four months since the Home Secretary signed a payment-by-results deal with France to stop migrants leaving its beaches for Britain.

Amid the fanfare, we were told the first tranche of cash would fund around 1,000 officers to patrol the coast and intercept boats in shallow water.



Yet since then, more than 5,000 migrants have still managed to cross the Channel and land on our shores.

So if this really is payment by results, perhaps the French should be paying US.



Paris is keen to boast that its efforts have stopped 46,000 asylum seekers making the perilous journey since 2024.

But what British taxpayers are seeing is rather different.



We’ve seen French officers tossing life jackets into overcrowded dinghies, giving boats a helping shove and waving them on their way towards Britain.

And today we reveal the extraordinary sight of French officials on a jetski only intercepting a dinghy heading for England because its engine had failed.

Up to that point officials simply stood and watched as the boat filled up with around 100 migrants.

The French appear to be getting money for old tow rope while Britain gets the bill.



This is a slap in the face to hard- working British taxpayers who have been forced to stump up £1billion to France, only to be told that more undocumented migrants will continue arriving on our shores and moving into communities already under pressure.

Enough is enough.

Britain needs some straight talking with our French friends.

If they want our money, they need to show us real results — not rubber dinghies being rubber-stamped on their way towards Dover.

Stop the boats. Stop the excuses. And start delivering what British taxpayers are paying for.



Because next time France comes knocking for another cheque, there should be just one answer:

Jet offski!

Tragic errors

TIME and again after tragedy strikes we are assured that “lessons will be learned”.

But all too often they never are.

Those words of comfort were trotted out earlier this year after it emerged that Southport killer Axel Rudakubana had been referred three times to the Prevent anti-terror programme.



But today we learn that teachers and other professionals who flag up their concerns are being met with “closed doors and dead ends”.

Four out of five of the 4,715 child referrals last year were quickly brushed off, according to the Children’s Commissioner.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Our safeguarding teams have experienced far too many lessons written in blood.

How many more tragedies must we witness before they learn?

News.title: Inside UK’s gangster football team with train robber & brutal enforcer who ripped out teeth…before gunfight stopped play
News.content:
IF Leeds United’s Norman Hunter liked to “bite yer legs” and Chelsea’s Ron Harris chopped down players like firewood, spare a thought for the opponents of the infamous Soho Rangers.

The team included first-division robbers and gangsters from the 1960s connected to the Richardson crime syndicate, who were notorious for their brutal torture techniques.



Gang boss Eddie Richardson, who last week died aged 90, led the attack. And “Mad” Frankie Fraser played left-back, making Vinnie Jones’ grab of Paul Gascoigne’s crown jewels look positively tame compared to his prowess with a pair of pliers.

In goal was Danny Pembroke, one of the Great Train robbers who was never caught for the 1963 heist.

Pembroke was famed in the underworld for always wearing gloves — and kept a clean sheet of the ­criminal variety.



Soho Rangers were managed by renowned gangland figure and Mr Fixit Albert Dimes, who had close connections to the US Mafia.

Their number one fan and co-manager was hell-raising actor and Zulu star Stanley Baker, a mobster’s pal and close friend of most of the team.

With the new football season now under way, and the Premier League opening at the weekend, The Sun today looks back at Britain’s hardest ever team.

Not all Soho Rangers members were crooks and a few went on to lead successful and legitimate lives.

One player, boxing manager Bert McCarthy, had Nigel Benn on his books as a young fighter, before going on to make a fortune in microchips.



But many of the team were habitual criminals.

Soho Rangers’ history was short-lived, ending abruptly following a notorious underworld fight at the bizarrely named Mr Smith’s And The Witch Doctor club in Catford, South London.

The Richardson gang had been “invited” by the management to take over the club and install their fruit machines, which a rival South ­London gang took exception to.

Two players, “Mad” Frankie and Ronnie Jeffreys, were shot in the March 1966 carnage, in which rival Kray gang associate Dickie Hart died.



The genesis of Soho Rangers was Westminster FC, a Sunday league team set up by Richardson and his South London boyhood friend Arthur Baron, in the early 1960s.

They played at the Grassmeade home ground of non-league team Cray Wanderers, which Arthur went on to successfully manage.

The team also played charity matches and Eddie told how they assembled the squad from workers in the scrap metal business he ran with his brother Charlie, “and a few real good players, including a one-time Queens Park Rangers forward . . .”

He recalled in his autobiography: “After one season we were in the First Division. I got us fitted out in a full red strip and I used to race around in it as centre forward.”



He said his brother Charlie never played, “but he’d turn out to watch the games.”

“It was fun and relaxing and it brought the lads together at weekends,” he added.

Eddie also set up a team called The Lonsdales, after the Soho-based sports equipment firm, to play against a side of prisoners at top-security Parkhurst jail on the Isle of Wight.

Borrowing Lonsdale notepaper, Eddie wrote to the prison governor offering to play against the prison team and a match was arranged.



As well as Eddie, Lonsdale also included boxer Terry Spinks, Richardson firm member Ronnie Jeffreys, ex-fighter Terry Murphy, whose actor son Glen later starred in London’s Burning, and Mad Frankie.

Eddie’s description of the match in his book, No Handcuffs: The Final Word On My War With The Krays, mirrored the classic scene from TV comedy Porridge featuring a prison football game.

He wrote: “Some of the lads inside knew we were coming, but nobody let on that they recognised us.

“We got changed into our strip and went out on to the pitch.



“All the prisoners were out on exercise so they all came to watch. We kept up the pretence until half time, when they all swarmed on to the pitch to shake hands and chat.

“We had lots of tobacco and ­cigarettes in our bags to give them, and they were all stuffing letters in our hands to take out with us.

“Of course, the screws knew then what was going on, but there was ­little they could do.

“They let us play the second half, because they couldn’t really stop it. The prison team took it seriously — they beat us 3-1. The prison staff had laid on a tea for us afterwards.

“But there was no way they were going to let us stay a minute longer than they could avoid.



“We were hustled out as soon as we got changed after the match.”

Eddie and his pal Leslie McCarthy formed the notorious Soho Rangers.

The photo of the team was taken before a match against a squad of national newspaper and sports journalists at Cray Wanderers’ ground, believed to have taken place in 1965. On the far left of the back row, wearing a trilby hat, shirt and tie, was hard-living Welsh actor ­Stanley Baker.



Richardson said: “Stanley was a mate. I’d met him a few times in Soho through Albert Dimes.

“He was a man’s man and liked hanging around with hard men.

“He knew but ‘there for the grace of God, go I.’

“He told me that if his acting career hadn’t taken off the way it did, he could easily have been a villain.” To his right was Billy Rawlings, brother of Richardson’s close friend Harry, who survived being shot in the Mr Smith’s club battle.

Next to him was Reggie “The ­Milkman” Saunders, who delivered pints before going to work for the Richardsons at their scrapyard.



With his hand down his shorts next to him was George Wisbey, brother of Great Train Robber Tommy Wisbey, who went on to run a successful greengrocery business in South London.

Standing in the middle of the back row with arms folded was keeper Danny Pembroke, who was arrested but never charged over the Great Train robbery.

As Richardson appropriately noted of his keeper: “Danny had worn gloves for every moment that mattered during and after the robbery.”

Pembroke was apparently cheated out of much of his take from the ­famous robbery and later became a London cabbie.

He died aged 79 in 2015 and a blown-up photo of the Soho Rangers was “given pride of place on the wall” at his wake. “It was quite a team,” said Richardson.



To Pembroke’s right in the picture was Billy Staynton, a Richardson gang member, jail breaker and villain.

Staynton stood trial twice with Richardson for affray over the club incident before being acquitted along with hitman Jimmy Moody and apparently going straight.

Alongside Staynton in the photo was Tommy McCarthy, who ran the Log Cabin bar in Soho, the unofficial HQ of the Richardson gang.

Standing behind him was Albert Dimes, a bookmaker and gambler nicknamed “Italian Albert”.

Dimes was a close friend of Billy ‘The King of the Underworld’ Hill and famously had a Soho fight involving razors with Hill’s enemy Jack “Spot” Comer. Family man Dimes was connected to the Mafia and involved in the Richardson gang fruit machine business. Richardson said of him: “He was a big guy, over 6ft tall, and he had a presence.



“He was like the League Of Nations in Soho — everyone took their problems to Albert to sort out.”

The central character played by Stanley Baker in the 1960 crime film, The Criminal, was based on Soho gangster Dimes.

But his soccer skills were lacking and the first time Dimes ever played he did not even know how to take a throw in.

Last in the back row was “Mad” Frankie Fraser, who spent a total of 42 years in prison.

Fraser’s speciality was ripping out teeth with pliers and electrocuting rivals’ testicles with a hand-operated generator.



Arsenal fan Fraser was shot in the thigh during the Mr Smith’s club fight and received five years for affray over that.

He later got ten years at the 1967 Richardson torture trial and went on to lead the Parkhurst jail riot — whose pitch he previously graced.

Fraser was given an ASBO aged 89 in 2013 following a row at his care home and died the following year.

Sitting on the far left of the front row was boxing manager Bert McCarthy, believed to be related to teammate Tommy and a friend of the Richardson family.

The Essex businessman managed Nigel Benn during his younger career, as well as ring legends Errol Christie and Terry Marsh.



McCarthy made a fortune from microchips and in 1982 took an ­associate to court over a contract wrangle around Frank Bruno.

Next in line was Millwall fan Eddie Richardson, whose love of the beautiful game contrasted with the torture techniques employed by his brother Charlie and Fraser.

Richardson was released on bail on July 26, 1966, over the Mr Smith’s club fight earlier that year.

He had tickets to attend England’s World Cup Final four days later, but was arrested when Scotland Yard swooped on the Richardson gang that morning.

Richardson was later convicted of affray and got five years, and was sentenced to another ten years for GBH following the torture trial.



He was jailed again in 1989 for 25 years for conspiracy to import drugs and served 12 years before release.

Sitting to his right in the photo is Peter Warner, a friend of Eddie Richardson’s boyhood friend Arthur Baron.

There is no suggestion he was involved in any criminality.

To his right was Ronnie Jeffreys, who was blasted in the groin and stomach during the battle at Mr Smith’s club.

Jeffreys, credited with trying to stop the gunfight which continued out on to the street, was cleared of affray over the incident. Last in line to the right was Ronnie Oliver, looking down away from the camera.



He is believed to have been a friend of the Richardsons and has never been linked to any criminality.

The Soho Rangers left Scotland Yard bemused.

Retired Met detective chief inspector Mick Neville said: “The team were working-class lads and naturally loved their football.

“But I doubt whether there has been a line-up quite like it outside of a police ID parade.

“Wimbledon FC used to be called the ‘Crazy Gang’, but with ‘Mad’ Frankie on the teamsheet, Soho ­Rangers was even more insane.



“Some of this team didn’t just grab an opponent’s testicles, like Vinnie Jones did to Gazza — they electrocuted them.”

Mr Neville added: “Had any crooks in the team shown any promise as footballers, there would have been only one club for them -— Aston Villain!”

News.title: UK wildfire risk remains critical despite forecast of heavy rain as fire chiefs warn ‘we’re not out of this yet’
News.content:
BONE-DRY Britain’s wildfire risk remains critical despite the forecast of heavy downpours this week.

Fire chiefs said exhausted crews have tackled a record-breaking 1,132 fires this year.



And although the number of outbreaks is beginning to drop, they insisted: “We are not out of this yet.”

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner yesterday visited 19 homes which were destroyed last week.



She walked among the ruins in Stourbridge, West Mids, after flames tore through the area and said: “It was like going through a movie — I’ve never seen that level of devastation.”

Other fires have raged in the past few days across South Wales, in the New Forest, Stoke-on-Trent and in the Cairngorms in Scotland.



In Sunderland, aerial images captured firefighters tackling a blaze which destroyed 80 tons of straw.

It was started deliberately by children and ripped through 40 acres of land at Flinton Hill Farm on Sunday.

Farm manager Tania Coxon, 29, said: “It’s not actually shocking to us, pretty much every year we have fires that are set by kids.

“There’s nothing the police can do. The kids just disappear into the woods and nothing ever gets done about it. Normally we can get the fires under control quite easily but we weren’t able to with this one.”



Phil Garrigan, of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Conditions remain exceptionally dry in many parts of the country and it only takes one spark to start a serious wildfire.”

He added: “The progress we are seeing is encouraging, but continued public support and responsibility will be critical in the days ahead. We are not out of this yet.”

Half of England is now in drought after five heatwaves.



However, temperatures began to cool yesterday ahead of long-awaited rainfall. The Met Office said showers from today would be followed by heavy downpours for much of the UK on Thursday.

News.title: ‘Devastated’ family of bus driver, 25, share heartbreaking tribute after ‘amazing’ man shot dead outside pub
News.content:
THE family of a bus driver who was shot dead have paid tribute to him – an “amazing man” who brought “joy” to others.

Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa, 25, known in the area as “Billy”, was arriving home from work when he was killed outside a pub in Clapham on August 10.



Cops and paramedics scrambled to the Landor Pub just before 10pm after receiving reports of gunfire.

Despite paramedics arriving within three minutes, he was pronounced dead at the scene with Billy’s friends saying he was in the “wrong place at the wrong time”.



Following the tragedy, his family have paid a touching tribute.

They said: “We are devastated by the horrific murder of Bile-aka. He was an amazing young man full of love, kindness, and an enthusiasm for life.



“Bile-aka touched so many hearts, and the pain of losing him is impossible to put into words.

“It is difficult to imagine a world without his smile, his presence, and the joy he brought to those around him.



“Family, friends, and colleagues are heartbroken, and all we want now is justice for him.

“Please stand with us and help us honour Bile-aka by making sure his life is remembered and that justice is served.”

The Sun has seen CCTV footage showing a male wearing a moped helmet limping with “blood pouring out his mouth.”

It shows the man walking down a high road about a minute from the scene of the shooting.

The male limping is understood to be a 22-year-old male who presented himself to hospital with a gunshot wound.



At the time of the incident, police arrested a man, 22, on suspicion of murder, but no further arrests have been made.

The Met has now renewed an appeal to the public for information on the shooting and continues its urgent enquiries.

Detective Chief Inspector Claire Guiver, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts remain with Bile-aka’s family as they continue to come to terms with this tragic incident.

“We are extending our appeal to members of the public, and anyone in the area around the time of the shooting to please come forward.

“Any piece of information you have could prove vital in our investigation. If you witnessed anything suspicious, or have CCTV, dashcam or doorbell footage that could assist our investigation, we urge you to get in touch.



“No matter how big or small, your information could be crucial in our investigation.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information is encouraged to contact police on 101 quoting reference 8379/10AUG.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Water companies want to hike our bills while RATIONING how much we use – why Burnham must not let it happen
News.content:
HOW typical of the water industry to exploit the current drought to try to push for the right to impose “surge pricing” on its customers.

Ofwat, the regulator, has proposed that companies be allowed to charge more ­during periods of low rainfall.



Funny enough, though, water companies are not planning to slash bills during wet periods when their reservoirs are brimming.

They just want an excuse to push up our bills even further, while trying to ration water so they don’t have to invest much in new infrastructure, or in mending their leaky pipes.



It is true, of course, that July and August have been exceptionally dry.

Our parks have turned brown and our gardens are wilting. But Britain remains a country with a damp, temperate climate.

Water companies are counting on us having short memories. Actually, we had an even wetter winter than usual.

In January, England saw 150 per cent of its average rainfall in that month.

February had 170 per cent. June, too, saw above-average rainfall.

Over the year as a whole, there has been plenty of rain to top up reservoirs and replenish ground water.



It is just that we don’t have the ­infrastructure to store enough of it for use during dry periods.

Travel to the Pennines or the Welsh Hills and you can see the magnificent dams and reservoirs constructed between Victorian times and the mid-20th Century.

But that investment has come to a ­shuddering halt in the past few decades.

The last significant reservoir constructed in Britain, Kielder Water in Northumberland, was completed in 1981.

At the same time, water companies are still losing vast quantities of their product to leaks.



Every day, 3,000million litres, or about 20 per cent of all treated water, goes missing before it even reaches the consumer.

Water companies claim they have reduced this by 40 per cent since privatisation, but they should have done far better than that.

They inherited a system of cast iron water mains laid in Victorian times and which were coming to the end of their lives.



With the new materials they now have available, they should have reduced ­leakage to a tiny fraction of what it was 40 years ago.

Why bother, they seem to calculate, when we could just ration the water supply instead, through regular hosepipe bans and now, it seems, through surge pricing?

In no other kind of industry are businesses so reluctant to sell us their product.

Can you imagine Tesco telling its ­customers they could only buy half a dozen rashers of bacon a week or jacking up the price of carrots in a deliberate bid to dissuade us from buying them?

Supermarkets do sometimes find themselves short of certain products, but they will scour the Earth to find replacements.



They invest in their supply chains — they don’t shake their heads and tell us sorry, we can’t have any food today because it is too much bother for them to go out and find any to offer us.

And they certainly don’t let 20 per cent of their food fall out of the back of their lorries before it even reaches the shops.

I have no rosy view of nationalised industry, and I remember how state-owned water companies struggled in the drought of 1976, forcing standpipes on some ­neighbourhoods.

But it was a big mistake to privatise the water industry without ensuring there was some kind of ­competition in place. It was an error, too, to privatise the assets.

Within years, much of the water industry had fallen into the hands of private equity groups who mortgaged the ­reservoirs, the sewers, and all the other infrastructure which had been built with taxpayers’ money, and awarded themselves big paydays.



They loaded themselves with debt, ­making the calculation that the government would never allow them to go bust because it would cause too much ­disruption to the water supply.

Water companies have done the same to the sewers as they have to the water ­supply: failed properly to invest in them.

The result is that we still have raw ­sewage being released into rivers during periods of heavy rain.

This is not entirely the fault of the ­people currently running the water industry: the problem goes back to a fateful ­decision in Victorian times to combine storm drains (which remove water from the streets when there is a downpour) with foul drains (which remove waste water and sewage from buildings).

This means that when there is heavy rain, sewage treatment works are overloaded and effluent bypasses them.



But water companies have done next to nothing to start work on separating the two systems.

They appear to have made the cold calculation that it is cheaper for them to pay the fines rather than invest in new sewers. The result is dead rivers and foul beaches.

PM Andy Burnham has said he wants to exert more public control over the water industry. It is unclear exactly what he means by this.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But please can he not go down the route of rationing.

A clean water supply is an essential ­element of any civilisation, and neither government nor the water industry should be trying to stop us using what we need.

News.title: Brit shot while driving in Jamaica flees to airport for safety before collapsing inside ‘in scene out of a movie’
News.content:
GUNMEN HORROR Brit shot while driving in Jamaica flees to airport for safety before collapsing inside ‘in scene out of a movie’

A BRITISH driver was shot during a horror drive-by gun attack before fleeing to an airport and collapsing in front of shocked bystanders.

Stunned witnesses said the dramatic scenes were like a “movie” as the 33-year-old victim rushed his bullet-riddled vehicle to the arrivals terminal in Jamaica.



The Brit tried to escape by dashing into Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, St James, on August 10 at around 9:30pm local time.

He was travelling with his partner and two Jamaican relatives on Queen’s Drive when the attack unfolded.



His vehicle stopped at a traffic light before another car pulled up alongside it and opened fire, local police said.

The Brit was shot in the upper section of his body.



He then went on to drive his vehicle to the airport – stopping at arrivals before running inside.

The wounded man fell down in front of horrified travellers, many of whom had just arrived from the UK, according to local media.

He was reportedly screaming for help as he came in.

A fellow Brit of Jamaican origin said: “There were lots of Brits arriving on flights from the UK and people were wondering what was happening.



“The incident could have almost looked like a movie scene if it was not real.”

Police rushed to the scene and took the injured Brit to hospital.

His current condition is not known.

The Brit is a forex trader, according to local media.

It is unclear why the shooting took place and whether any other passengers were wounded during the horror.



Police have launched an investigation into the full circumstances of the attack.

But investigators have not disclosed a possible motive or stated whether they believe it was a targeted assault.

There were reportedly multiple bullet holes left in the side of the Brit’s Subaru car.

The Sun reached out to Jamaica Constabulary Force for comment.

News.title: Restaurant’s bizarre air conditioning ruse leaves internet VERY confused – can you see what’s happening?
News.content:
In this day and age, the lack of air conditioning in a tourist attraction can be a dealbreaker during sweltering summers.

So it is no shock that management will go to any lengths to attract people – even if that means installing a “cyber AC”.



The unusual display was spotted at the outdoor waiting area of the Only Henan Drama Fantasy City attraction in Zhengzhou, central China.

Footage shows an AC on the screen appearing to blow streams of cool air towards visitors waiting beneath a shelter.



A fan is also seen spinning, creating the appearance of cooling equipment operating in the outdoor queue.

Some social media users reacted by saying: “Even the cyber AC can feel it.”



Others joked: “What kind of abstract thing is the attraction playing?”

The attraction finally responded to the online heat by explaining that the screen was deliberately used in the outdoor waiting area.

A member of staff said the area had a sunshade and was equipped with several real electric fans for visitors waiting outside.

“All the indoor theatres in the park are equipped with air conditioning and are open throughout the day,” they added.



They said that the virtual AC was not intended to replace the real cooling equipment, but was designed to soothe visitors and help them cope with the heat while queuing.

The attraction said: “The purpose of playing the air conditioner blowing air on the big screen is only to ease the irritability of tourists waiting in the heat.”

Staff later clarified that the virtual cooling display was only shown when temperatures exceeded 35C.

When temperatures fell in the days after the footage was recorded, the electronic screen was switched to other content.

Temperatures in Zhengzhou hover around the mid-30C during the summer, but have reached 40C in the past.
